mcqs.question: An `Order` class checks `if (status === 'shipped')` at the top of `cancel()`, `ship()`, and `refund()` separately. What's the risk as new statuses are added?
options: A new status like 'returned' has to be threaded into every method's checks, and missing one silently allows an invalid action
None — as long as each method is short the duplication is harmless
TypeScript will refuse to compile code with more than three status checks
The Order class will automatically become slower with each new status
mcqs.explanation: The real risk is duplicated status logic scattered across methods — adding a new status means finding and updating every place that checks it, and missing one produces a silent bug like a 'cancellable' delivered order. There's no compiler limit on status checks, and correctness, not raw performance, is the actual concern.

mcqs.question: A feature flag has exactly two states, `on` and `off`, that have not changed in years. Per this topic's guidance, what's the better implementation?
options: A full State pattern with OnState/OffState classes, since it's always more correct than a boolean
State pattern is mandatory any time there is more than one possible value
A plain boolean or two-value enum with a simple check — State's class overhead isn't worth it here
Neither approach works; feature flags require a separate architectural pattern entirely
mcqs.explanation: For a 2-state machine that rarely changes, a boolean or simple enum is clearer and has no real downside — this is exactly the case the topic flags as not worth State's extra classes. State pattern isn't mandatory by value count, and a boolean is a completely standard way to model a flag.

mcqs.question: In a Navigator class, calling `navigator.getDirections()` never changes which RouteStrategy object the Navigator holds — only an external call to `setStrategy()` does. What does this confirm?
options: This is State, because a context holds an object behind a shared interface
This is neither pattern, since no state machine is present
This is State, because RouteStrategy has more than one implementation
This is Strategy — the held object never changes itself; only external code reassigns it
mcqs.explanation: The deciding signal is who changes the currently-held object: here, calling a method on the strategy never causes it to be replaced — only an outside caller's setStrategy() does. That's Strategy's defining trait, even though the class shapes of State and Strategy are identical. Having multiple implementations of an interface doesn't by itself indicate a state machine.

mcqs.question: A workflow has 15 states and dozens of valid transitions between them, each implemented as a separate State class. What problem does this pitfall warn about?
options: State pattern cannot be used for more than 5 states under any circumstances
Distributing complex transition logic across 15 small classes can make the overall machine harder to see at a glance than one explicit transition table
15 classes will always run slower than a single switch statement
This is not a real problem — more classes are always easier to maintain than fewer
mcqs.explanation: State pattern doesn't eliminate the inherent complexity of a large state machine — it distributes it across many files, which can hide the overall picture that a single explicit transition table or a dedicated state-machine library would show clearly. There's no hard class-count limit, and runtime speed isn't the concern here.
